title: Independence supplies the exponent
question: Why is the probability f to the power n, rather than just f?
recap: For n independent uniformly distributed points, the chance that all lie in a fraction f of a volume is fⁿ. Perfectly locked positions instead give f; the exponent is a statement about independence.
premises: Each point is uniformly distributed over the initial volume.
The point positions are statistically independent for the independent model.
Entropy differences are related to logarithms of relative configuration probabilities.
limitations: The locked-position example is an authored mathematical counterexample, not an established alternative theory of radiation.
Spontaneous concentration probability and constrained-state entropy are related but are not the same observable.

overview.text: For n independent uniformly distributed points, the chance that all lie in a fraction f of a volume is fⁿ. Perfectly locked positions instead give f; the exponent is a statement about independence.

full.text: Each independent point has probability f of being inside the chosen fraction. For all n to be inside, multiply n independent probabilities. Taking the logarithm makes the exponent n a coefficient.

full.returnCaption: Return to why the entropy is the logarithm of the probability.

full.spoken: The probability is f to the n; the entropy difference is Boltzmann's constant times its logarithm, or n times Boltzmann's constant times the logarithm of f.

full.text: With four independent points and half the volume, the probability is 1/16. If all four positions are exactly the same uniformly distributed position, the probability is 1/2 instead. Having four labels is not enough to justify four independent factors.

The concentration from V₀ to V smaller than V₀ has a negative entropy difference. Reversing the constrained comparison reverses the sign. The independent-configurations laboratory makes the probability and entropy readouts separate.

full.returnCaption: Return to the independence assumption behind the volume exponent.

steps.returnCaption: Return to the chance that all n points are in the chosen part.

steps.text: Letters: the paper writes W for the probability of a state and \(S-S_0=\frac{R}{N}\lg W\) for Boltzmann's principle, and for the case below \(W=(v/v_0)^n\). This explanation writes f for \(v/v_0\) and \(k_B\) for R/N.

items: Boltzmann's principle, as the paper states it: the entropy of a system is a function of the probability of its state. For two systems that do not act on each other, the entropies add and the probabilities multiply. A function that turns products into sums is a logarithm, so the entropy is C times ln W plus a constant, and the paper takes C = R/N from the kinetic theory of gases.

The setting: n movable points in a volume \(v_0\), so few that they do not act on each other, with no part of the space and no direction preferred. They could be the molecules of a dilute gas or of a dissolved substance.
The question: at a moment chosen at random, what is the probability that all n points are in a chosen part v of \(v_0\)?
One point is equally likely to be anywhere, so the chance that it is in v is the fraction of the volume, \(f=v/v_0\).
Two independent points are both inside with probability f × f. For n independent points, multiply n times: \(W=f^n\).
Worked case: n = 4 and f = 1/2. Mark each point as in or out: there are 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 equally likely patterns, and exactly one has all four in, so W = 1/16, which is \((1/2)^4\).
Take the logarithm: \(\ln W=n\ln f\). In the worked case, \(\ln(1/16)=4\ln(1/2)\), about -2.77.
Multiply by \(k_B\), the paper's R/N, to get the entropy difference.

steps.returnCaption: Return to why the entropy is the logarithm of the probability.

steps.spoken: The probability is f to the n; the entropy difference is Boltzmann's constant times its logarithm, or n times Boltzmann's constant times the logarithm of f.

items: In the paper's letters this is \(S-S_0=R\frac{n}{N}\lg\frac{v}{v_0}\). Here n/N is the number of gram-molecules of points, so R times it is the gas constant for that amount.

A footnote draws the gas law from it: the work \(p\,dv\) equals \(T\,dS=R\frac{n}{N}\frac{dv}{v}\), so \(pv=R\frac{n}{N}T\), the law of Boyle and Gay-Lussac and the same law for osmotic pressure. The paper remarks that no assumption about how the molecules move was needed.

Independence is doing the work. If the four points were locked to one shared position, the chance of finding all of them in half the volume would be 1/2, not 1/16. Four labels do not by themselves give four independent factors.
The sign: concentrating the points into a smaller part (f less than 1) makes ln f negative, so the concentrated state has the lower entropy. Reversing the comparison reverses the sign.

steps.returnCaption: Return to the independence assumption behind the volume exponent.

margin.text: This is Boltzmann’s principle read backwards. Einstein computes how the entropy of dilute radiation changes with volume, compares it with the entropy of \(n\) independent points, \(k\ln W\) with \(W = f^n\), and concludes that such radiation behaves thermodynamically as if it consisted of \(n\) independent energy quanta. For large \(n\), \(f^n\) is astronomically small, so the laboratory reports its logarithm.
